mcqs.question: Why does `Board.resolvePosition(rawPosition)` get called on every turn, even when a player lands on an ordinary empty cell?
options: Because the jump map would otherwise become corrupted after repeated reads
Because calling it conditionally would require the turn loop to know which cells are snakes or ladders, re-coupling the exact concerns the design separates
Because Dice.roll() depends on the previous call to resolvePosition
Because it recalculates the board's total cell count on every call
mcqs.explanation: Calling resolvePosition unconditionally means the turn loop never needs to know board content — it just trusts the return value, whether that's a jump or the same cell back. Making the call conditional on cell content would require the loop to inspect the board itself, undoing the separation of concerns. The jump map is read-only lookup data here, and Dice.roll() has no dependency on board resolution.

mcqs.question: Why does making `Dice` an interface (with a `FakeDice` for tests) matter for this design?
options: It's required because Java forbids classes that generate random numbers
It makes the game run faster in production
It allows a test to assert an exact, reproducible game trace by scripting a fixed sequence of rolls instead of relying on genuine randomness
It removes the need for a Board class in unit tests
mcqs.explanation: A scripted FakeDice lets a test assert a precise sequence of outcomes deterministically — real randomness makes that impossible to reproduce. There's no such Java restriction, this isn't a production performance optimization, and Board is still needed to resolve positions regardless of which Dice implementation is used.

mcqs.question: A player at position 97 rolls a 5, which would put them at raw position 102 on a 100-cell board. Under the standard exact-roll rule, what should `resolvePosition` return?
options: 100, capping the player at the final cell so they win
102, allowing the position to exceed the board size
2, wrapping the overshoot around past the final cell
97, the player's unchanged position — the turn passes with no movement
mcqs.explanation: Under the exact-roll rule, a roll that would overshoot the final cell doesn't move the player at all — they stay at their current position and the turn simply passes. Capping at 100 incorrectly grants an early win, allowing 102 breaks the board's bounds, and wrapping past the end isn't part of the standard rule set.
